## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Samaṇamuṇḍika Sutta* (MN 78; PTS MN ii 22) is set in a debate hall built by Queen Mallikā for religious discussions [Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. The sutta centres on a dialogue triggered by the wanderer Uggāhamāna Samaṇamaṇḍikāputta, who asserts that a person reaches the highest attainment simply by observing four basic ethical precepts; the Buddha refutes this minimalistic criterion, setting forth considerably higher ethical and mental requirements [SuttaCentral]. In doing so, the Buddha underscores that non-harming is an indispensable facet of wholesomeness (*kusala*) and that unwholesome states inevitably produce harm and suffering [Goodwin 2012]. The text further analyzes the progressive cessation of mental resolves across meditative absorption, noting that unwholesome intentions subside in the first *jhāna* while wholesome intentions cease in the second *jhāna* [Polak 2011].
